marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q001.takeaway: Low SHBG most increases the free fraction of testosterone because much circulating testosterone is normally protein-bound.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q001.displayText:
Low SHBG most increases the free fraction of testosterone because much circulating testosterone is normally protein-bound.

The decrease in sex hormone-binding globulin will have the maximum effect on testosterone.

Around 98% of the circulating testosterone is bound to plasma proteins such as sex hormone-binding globulin (65%) and albumin. So, the decrease in sex-hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) or gonadal steroid-binding globulin (GBG) will have the maximum effect on testosterone levels by increasing the levels of its free form.

Therefore patients with polycystic ovary syndrome will show features of hyperandrogenism (due to elevated free testosterone).
emphasis: Low SHBG most increases the free fraction of testosterone because much circulating testosterone is normally protein-bound

rationales.a: Estrogen also binds SHBG, but the greatest clinically relevant change in this setting is free testosterone.
rationales.c: DHEA binds less avidly to SHBG and is largely sulfated; its free fraction is less affected.
rationales.d: Progesterone is not the major SHBG-bound sex steroid in this comparison.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q002.takeaway: Sertoli cells express FSH receptors; LH receptors are primarily on Leydig cells.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q002.displayText:
Sertoli cells express FSH receptors; LH receptors are primarily on Leydig cells.

Sertoli cells express FSH receptor, whereas Leydig cells express LH receptor.

Sertoli cells are the true epithelial cells of the seminiferous epithelium and extend from basal lamina to the lumen.

Functions of Sertoli cells:
• Express FSH receptor and androgen receptor.
• Form the blood-testis barrier.
• Surround the sperm cells and provide structural support within the epithelium.
• Guide sperm cells towards the lumen as they advance to later stages of spermatogenesis.
• Produce inhibin and Mullerian-inhibiting substance (MIS).
• Produce androgen-binding proteins that maintain high androgen levels within the lumen of the seminiferous tubules and the proximal part of the male reproductive tract.
• Perform phagocytic function by engulfing residual bodies (cytoplasm shed by spermatozoa during spermiogenesis) and dead sperm cells.
• Express aromatase, which converts testosterone to potent estrogen.
emphasis: Sertoli cells express FSH receptors; LH receptors are primarily on Leydig cells

rationales.b: LH acts on Leydig cells to stimulate testosterone synthesis.
rationales.c: Inhibin is secreted by Sertoli cells and feeds back at pituitary, but is not their receptor answer.
rationales.d: GnRH receptors are on pituitary gonadotrophs, not Sertoli cells.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q003.takeaway: Sertoli-cell inhibin B selectively suppresses pituitary FSH secretion.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q003.displayText:
Sertoli-cell inhibin B selectively suppresses pituitary FSH secretion.

The negative feedback mechanism involving the Sertoli cells causes ↓FSH.

FSH stimulates inhibin production by the Sertoli cells. This inhibin inhibits FSH production by directly acting on the anterior pituitary. Thus, inhibin keeps FSH levels within a set point.
emphasis: Sertoli-cell inhibin B selectively suppresses pituitary FSH secretion

rationales.a: LH is chiefly feedback-inhibited by testosterone from Leydig cells.
rationales.c: TRH regulates TSH and prolactin, not the Sertoli feedback loop.
rationales.d: CRH regulates ACTH, unrelated to Sertoli-cell inhibin feedback.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q004.takeaway: LH stimulates Leydig cells to synthesize and secrete testosterone.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q004.displayText:
LH stimulates Leydig cells to synthesize and secrete testosterone.

In men, LH controls the secretion of testosterone.

LH stimulates Leydig cells to secrete testosterone, which in turn inhibits LH by a negative feedback mechanism. FSH stimulates Sertoli cells to secrete inhibin, which in turn inhibits FSH by a negative feedback mechanism.

Testosterone inhibits LH secretion by acting directly on the anterior pituitary and by inhibiting the secretion of GnRH from the hypothalamus. Inhibin acts directly on the anterior pituitary to inhibit FSH secretion.

FSH also stimulates the secretion of ABP (androgen-binding protein) and inhibin. FSH and androgens maintain the gametogenic function of the testes. Hypothalamic lesions in animals and hypothalamic disease in humans lead to atrophy of the testes and loss of their function.
emphasis: LH stimulates Leydig cells to synthesize and secrete testosterone

rationales.a: Inhibin is produced by Sertoli cells in response to FSH, not controlled by LH as the principal answer.
rationales.b: Anti-Müllerian hormone is produced by Sertoli cells during fetal development.
rationales.d: Androgen-binding protein is produced by Sertoli cells under FSH/testosterone influence.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q005.takeaway: Leydig cells in the testicular interstitium are the principal source of testosterone.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q005.displayText:
Leydig cells in the testicular interstitium are the principal source of testosterone.

Testosterone production is mainly contributed by Leydig cells.

Testosterone is synthesized from cholesterol in the Leydig cells and also from androstenedione secreted by the adrenal cortex.

The diagnosis of testosterone deficiency should be made only on the basis of clinical signs and symptoms consistent with androgen deficiency, and consistently subnormal serum testosterone concentrations at 8 to 10 AM on three occasions.

Testosterone has been used to treat primary or secondary hypogonadism in adult men.
emphasis: Leydig cells in the testicular interstitium are the principal source of testosterone

rationales.b: Sertoli cells support germ cells and secrete inhibin/ABP; Leydig cells make most testosterone.
rationales.c: Seminiferous tubules house spermatogenesis, but testosterone is synthesized by interstitial Leydig cells.
rationales.d: Epididymis matures and stores sperm; it is not the primary testosterone-producing tissue.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q006.takeaway: 17α-hydroxyprogesterone is a steroid precursor, not an androgen; testosterone, DHT and androstenedione are androgens.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q006.displayText:
17α-hydroxyprogesterone is a steroid precursor, not an androgen; testosterone, DHT and androstenedione are androgens.

17° hydroxy-progesterone is a progestin, not an androgen.

The term androgen means any steroid hormone that has masculinizing effects. Testosterone, dihydrotestosterone, androstenedione, and dehydroepiandrosterone are androgens.

The sites of production:
• Testes.
• Adrenal gland.
• Ovary (not significant).
• Tumors of the adrenal androgen-producing cells etc.

Both in the testes and in the adrenals, the androgens can be synthesized either from cholesterol or directly from acetyl coenzyme A.
emphasis: 17α-hydroxyprogesterone is a steroid precursor, not an androgen; testosterone, DHT and androstenedione are androgens

rationales.c: Androstenedione is a weaker androgen and steroid precursor.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q007.takeaway: Anti-Müllerian hormone is secreted by fetal Sertoli cells and by granulosa cells of preantral/small antral follicles.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q007.displayText:
Anti-Müllerian hormone is secreted by fetal Sertoli cells and by granulosa cells of preantral/small antral follicles.

Anti Mullerian Hormone (AMH) is secreted by both Sertoli cells and granulosa cells.

Sertoli cells produce Anti Mullerian Hormone (Mullerian inhibitory substance) during development. It induces the regression of the Mullerian duct that is programmed to give rise to a female reproductive tract.

Granulosa cells of the ovary produce AMH during the reproductive years. It limits the formation of primary follicles by inhibiting excessive follicular recruitment by FSH.
emphasis: Anti-Müllerian hormone is secreted by fetal Sertoli cells and by granulosa cells of preantral/small antral follicles

rationales.a: Theca cells primarily synthesize androgens in response to LH.
rationales.b: Leydig cells make testosterone; fetal AMH is from Sertoli cells.
rationales.d: Müllerian ducts are targets of AMH, not the secreting cells.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q008.takeaway: Tight junctions between neighboring Sertoli cells form the blood–testis barrier and divide basal from adluminal compartments.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q008.displayText:
Tight junctions between neighboring Sertoli cells form the blood–testis barrier and divide basal from adluminal compartments.

The blood-testis barrier is formed by the tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells.

These Sertoli-Sertoli cell tight junctions divide the seminiferous epithelium into 2 compartments:
• Basal compartment - contains the spermatogonia and early-stage primary spermatocytes.
• Adluminal compartment - contains later-stage primary spermatocytes and all subsequent stages of sperm cells.

It imparts a selective permeability, allowing few substances such as testosterone to cross but preventing noxious substances that might damage the developing sperm. It also protects sperms from antibodies by creating a specialized, immunologically safe microenvironment for developing sperm.

BELOW DIAGRAM -
1 basal lamina, 2 spermatogonia, 3 spermatocyte 1st order, 4 spermatocyte 2nd order, 5 spermatid, 6 mature spermatid, 7 Sertoli cell, 8 tight junctions (Blood-Testis Barrier).
emphasis: Tight junctions between neighboring Sertoli cells form the blood–testis barrier and divide basal from adluminal compartments

rationales.a: Leydig cells lie outside seminiferous tubules and do not form the barrier.
rationales.c: Basal lamina and spermatogonia do not create the selective Sertoli junction barrier.
rationales.d: Leydig cells are interstitial; their basal lamina is not the blood–testis barrier.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q009.takeaway: Spermiogenesis is the remodeling of haploid spermatids into mature spermatozoa.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q009.displayText:
Spermiogenesis is the remodeling of haploid spermatids into mature spermatozoa.

Spermiogenesis refers to the formation of spermatozoa from spermatids.

Spermiogenesis is a process by which there is a formation of extremely specialized mobile spermatozoa from spermatids. This process requires extensive remodeling or packaging of cell elements. It occurs in the recesses formed by invaginations of the Sertoli cell plasma membrane.

Maturation from spermatids to spermatozoa depends on androgen acting on Sertoli cells. When sperm maturation is complete, the cytoplasm of the Sertoli cell around sperm retracts and sperms are released into the lumen to be bathed by the luminal fluid.

The following changes occur during the formation of spermatozoa from spermatids:
• The nucleus becomes eccentric and decreases in size, and the chromatin becomes condensed.
• The cytoplasmic content is redistributed and discarded.
• The acrosome buds from the Golgi apparatus.
• The centrioles migrate to the caudal pole and form a long axial filament made of microtubules. This becomes the axoneme or major portion of the tail.

Spermiation is the release of the sperm from the Sertoli cells. During spermiation, most of the remaining cytoplasm is shed in the form of residual bodies.

Spermatogenesis refers to the formation of spermatozoa from spermatogonia.
emphasis: Spermiogenesis is the remodeling of haploid spermatids into mature spermatozoa

rationales.a: Spermatogonia develop through mitosis and meiosis before forming spermatids.
rationales.c: Spermatids do not develop backward from sperm; spermiogenesis is their maturation into spermatozoa.
rationales.d: A primary-to-secondary spermatocyte transition is meiosis I, not spermiogenesis.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q010.takeaway: Human spermatogenesis takes roughly 70–75 days from spermatogonium to spermatozoon, with additional epididymal transit.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q010.displayText:
Human spermatogenesis takes roughly 70–75 days from spermatogonium to spermatozoon, with additional epididymal transit.

The time required to produce mature spermatozoa from the earliest stage of spermatogonia is 65 to 70 days.

Since several developmental stages of spermatogenic cells occur during this time frame, the stages are collectively known as the spermatogenic cycle.
emphasis: Human spermatogenesis takes roughly 70–75 days from spermatogonium to spermatozoon, with additional epididymal transit

rationales.a: 30–35 days is too short for the full spermatogenic sequence.
rationales.b: 40–45 days underestimates the time for germ-cell development.
rationales.c: 50–55 days remains shorter than the approximate 70–75-day duration.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q011.takeaway: Spermatogenesis depends on LH-driven testosterone and FSH actions on Sertoli cells, so all three listed hormones contribute.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q011.displayText:
Spermatogenesis depends on LH-driven testosterone and FSH actions on Sertoli cells, so all three listed hormones contribute.

All three of them (testosterone, FSH, LH) are required for spermatogenesis.

Pulses of hypothalamic GnRH stimulate the anterior pituitary to secrete FSH and LH, which then act on the testes.

FSH acts on the Sertoli cells to stimulate spermatogenesis and inhibin secretion. LH acts on the Leydig cells to stimulate testosterone secretion. Testosterone, acting locally on the Sertoli cells, is essential for maintaining spermatogenesis.
emphasis: Spermatogenesis depends on LH-driven testosterone and FSH actions on Sertoli cells, so all three listed hormones contribute

rationales.a: Testosterone supports germ-cell development within seminiferous tubules.
rationales.b: FSH stimulates Sertoli cells and supports spermatogenesis.
rationales.c: LH stimulates Leydig-cell testosterone production, which is required for spermatogenesis.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q012.takeaway: Growth hormone supports early spermatogonial mitotic divisions and normal testicular development.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q012.displayText:
Growth hormone supports early spermatogonial mitotic divisions and normal testicular development.

The growth hormone specifically promotes the early division of spermatogonia.

Hormonal factors that stimulate spermatogenesis:
• Testosterone, secreted by the Leydig cells of the testis, is essential for growth and division of the testicular germinal cells, which is the first stage in forming sperm.
• Luteinizing hormone, secreted by the anterior pituitary gland, stimulates the Leydig cells to secrete testosterone.
• Follicle-stimulating hormone, secreted by the anterior pituitary gland, stimulates the Sertoli cells. Without this stimulation, spermiogenesis will not occur.
• Estrogens, formed from testosterone by the Sertoli cells when stimulated by FSH, are also essential for spermiogenesis.
• Growth hormone is necessary for controlling the background metabolic functions of the testes. It specifically promotes early division of the spermatogonia themselves. In its absence, as in pituitary dwarfs, spermatogenesis is severely deficient or absent, thus causing infertility.
emphasis: Growth hormone supports early spermatogonial mitotic divisions and normal testicular development

rationales.a: FSH, not GH, is the primary direct Sertoli-cell stimulant.
rationales.c: Acrosome formation occurs during spermiogenesis in germ cells.
rationales.d: LH is the principal Leydig-cell stimulant; GH has an early germ-cell role.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q013.takeaway: Sertoli-cell inhibin provides negative feedback on pituitary FSH during spermatogenesis.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q013.displayText:
Sertoli-cell inhibin provides negative feedback on pituitary FSH during spermatogenesis.

Negative feedback in spermatogenesis is by inhibin.

FSH stimulates inhibin production by the Sertoli cells. This inhibin inhibits FSH production by directly acting on the anterior pituitary.

LH stimulates Leydig cells to secrete testosterone, which in turn inhibits LH. Testosterone inhibits LH secretion by acting directly on the anterior pituitary and by inhibiting the secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) from the hypothalamus.
emphasis: Sertoli-cell inhibin provides negative feedback on pituitary FSH during spermatogenesis

rationales.a: ABP concentrates testosterone in seminiferous tubules but is not the feedback hormone.
rationales.c: Progesterone is not the principal Sertoli feedback signal in male reproduction.
rationales.d: GnRH stimulates pituitary gonadotropins rather than providing negative feedback.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q014.takeaway: Varicocele warms the scrotum and impairs spermatogenesis because normal sperm production requires a temperature below core body temperature.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q014.displayText:
Varicocele warms the scrotum and impairs spermatogenesis because normal sperm production requires a temperature below core body temperature.

The most likely reason behind decreased sperm count in this patient is rise in scrotal temperature, secondary to varicocele.

Normally, the testes occupy the scrotum, which lies outside the body cavity and is maintained at 35° to 36°C, or 1° to 2°C below body temperature. This lower temperature is essential for normal spermatogenesis. It is maintained by a countercurrent arrangement of testicular arteries and veins, which facilitates heat exchange.

Enlarged veins around the testes, called varicoceles, cause infertility by raising the temperature in the scrotum and decreasing sperm production.
emphasis: Varicocele warms the scrotum and impairs spermatogenesis because normal sperm production requires a temperature below core body temperature

rationales.a: A lower scrotal temperature would favor, not impair, spermatogenesis.
rationales.c: Varicocele is a venous plexus dilation and temperature mechanism, not duct obstruction.
rationales.d: Vas deferens obstruction affects sperm transport but does not explain the varicocele finding.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q015.takeaway: Sperm acquire progressive motility during epididymal maturation.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q015.displayText:
Sperm acquire progressive motility during epididymal maturation.

Sperm is stored in the epididymis, where they undergo a process of maturation before they are capable of progressive motility and fertilization.

Changes during the sperm maturation in the epididymis:
• Progressive increase in forward motility
• Increase ability to fertilize
• Maturation of acrosome
• Molecular reorganization of plasma membrane: Lipid (stabilization of plasma membrane) protein (shedding as well as the acquisition of new proteins)
• Ability to bind to zona pellucida
• Acquisition of receptors for proteins of the zona pellucida
• Increase disulfide bond between cysteine residues in sperm nucleoproteins
• Topographic regionalization of glycosidic residues
• Accumulation of mannosylated residues on periacrosomal plasma membrane
• Decreased cytoplasm and cell volume
emphasis: Sperm acquire progressive motility during epididymal maturation

rationales.a: Seminal vesicles add fructose-rich fluid but do not mature sperm motility.
rationales.b: Sperm leave the testes immature and initially lack full motility.
rationales.d: The ejaculatory duct transports sperm and glandular secretions but is not where motility is acquired.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q016.takeaway: Capacitation occurs in the female reproductive tract, especially the uterine tubes, enabling sperm to fertilize the oocyte.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q016.displayText:
Capacitation occurs in the female reproductive tract, especially the uterine tubes, enabling sperm to fertilize the oocyte.

Capacitation of sperm takes place in uterine tubes.

Once ejaculated into the female genital tract, the spermatozoa move up the uterus to the isthmus of the uterine tubes, where they slow down and undergo final conditioning called capacitation.

This process involves two components:
• Increasing the motility of the spermatozoa
• Facilitating their preparation for the acrosomal reaction.
emphasis: Capacitation occurs in the female reproductive tract, especially the uterine tubes, enabling sperm to fertilize the oocyte

rationales.a: Seminiferous tubules produce sperm but do not capacitate them.
rationales.c: Epididymis enables maturation and motility, not female-tract capacitation.
rationales.d: The ejaculatory duct is a male transport passage, not the site of capacitation.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q017.takeaway: Female genital tract secretions support sperm motility and capacitation; acidic conditions and heat extremes impair motility.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q017.displayText:
Female genital tract secretions support sperm motility and capacitation; acidic conditions and heat extremes impair motility.

Sperm motility is increased by vaginal secretions.

On coming in contact with the fluids of the female genital tract, multiple changes occur that activate the sperm for the final processes of fertilization. These collective changes are called capacitation of the spermatozoa, which normally requires from 1 to 10 hours.

The following changes are believed to occur:
• The uterine and fallopian tube fluids wash away the various inhibitory factors that suppress sperm activity in the male genital ducts.
• While the spermatozoa remain in the fluid of the male genital ducts, they are continually exposed to many floating vesicles from the seminiferous tubules containing large amounts of cholesterol. This cholesterol is continually added to the cellular membrane covering the sperm acrosome, toughening this membrane and preventing the release of its enzymes.
• After ejaculation, the sperm deposited in the vagina swim away from the cholesterol vesicles upward into the uterine cavity, and they gradually lose much of their other excess cholesterol during the next few hours. In doing so, the membrane at the head of the sperm (the acrosome) becomes much weaker.
• The membrane of the sperm also becomes much more permeable to calcium ions, so calcium now enters the sperm in abundance and changes the activity of the flagellum, giving it a powerful whiplash motion in contrast to its previously weak undulating motion. In addition, the calcium ions cause changes in the cellular membrane that cover the leading edge of the acrosome, making it possible for the acrosome to release its enzymes rapidly and easily as the sperm penetrates the granulosa cell mass surrounding the ovum, and even more so as it attempts to penetrate the zona pellucida of the ovum.
emphasis: Female genital tract secretions support sperm motility and capacitation; acidic conditions and heat extremes impair motility

rationales.a: Higher temperature outside the optimal range can impair sperm function.
rationales.b: Vaginal acidity is hostile to sperm; cervical/uterine-tract secretions provide more favorable conditions.
rationales.d: Sperm within seminiferous tubules are immature and not yet motile.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q018.takeaway: Continuous GnRH agonist initially flares gonadotropins, then downregulates pituitary receptors and lowers LH with prolonged use.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q018.displayText:
Continuous GnRH agonist initially flares gonadotropins, then downregulates pituitary receptors and lowers LH with prolonged use.

Prolonged injection of GnRH will lead to decreased LH levels.

A constant administration of GnRH produces an initial agonistic action known as "flare", followed by a downregulation of GnRH receptors (decrease in GnRH receptor concentration). This desensitizes pituitary to the action of GnRH and a hypogonadotropic-hypogonadal state is induced.

This is characterized by low LH, low FSH levels and thereby reduced testosterone production (i.e., chemical castration).
emphasis: Continuous GnRH agonist initially flares gonadotropins, then downregulates pituitary receptors and lowers LH with prolonged use

rationales.a: FSH falls along with LH after chronic receptor downregulation, rather than increasing.
rationales.d: Lower LH reduces Leydig testosterone production.
